title: 7.0. LoRA Improvements in fine-tuning

7.0. LoRA Improvements in fine-tuning

LoRA Improvements

Tip

LoRA can substantially reduce the trainable parameter count and optimizer memory needed to fine-tune a pretrained model.

LoRA makes it possible to fine-tune large models efficiently by only changing a small part of the model. It reduces the number of parameters you need to train, saving memory and computational resources. This is because:[1]

  1. Reduces the number of trainable parameters: LoRA freezes the original weight W and represents an additive update as the product of two trainable low-rank matrices, commonly ΔW = B A, with rank r much smaller than the input/output dimensions.[3]

  2. This is because instead of calculating the complete weight update of a layer (matrix), it approximates it to a product of 2 smaller matrices reducing the update to calculate:\

  3. Keeps original model weights unchanged: Only the adapter matrices are optimized. Freezing weights prevents direct modification of the base checkpoint, although adapter behavior can still override or degrade knowledge at inference time.

  4. Efficient Task-Specific Fine-Tuning: When you want to adapt the model to a new task, you can just train the small LoRA matrices (A and B) while leaving the rest of the model as it is. This is much more efficient than retraining the entire model.
  5. Storage Efficiency: After fine-tuning, instead of saving a whole new model for each task, you only need to store the LoRA matrices, which are very small compared to the entire model. This makes it easier to adapt the model to many tasks without using too much storage.

The following minimal implementation adapts the cited notebook. It initializes B to zero so the adapter begins as a no-op, and uses the standard alpha / rank scaling from LoRA. The code stores the factors in input-major shapes (A is in_dim x rank and B is rank x out_dim), so its forward path is written as xAB; this is the transposed-shape equivalent of the paper's BA notation.[2][3]

import math
import torch

# Create the LoRA layer with the 2 matrices and the alpha
class LoRALayer(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim, rank, alpha):
        super().__init__()
        self.A = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.empty(in_dim, rank))
        torch.nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.A, a=math.sqrt(5))  # similar to standard weight initialization
        self.B = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(rank, out_dim))
        self.scaling = alpha / rank

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.scaling * (x @ self.A @ self.B)
        return x

# Combine it with the linear layer
class LinearWithLoRA(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, linear, rank, alpha):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = linear
        self.lora = LoRALayer(
            linear.in_features, linear.out_features, rank, alpha
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.linear(x) + self.lora(x)

# Replace linear layers with LoRA ones
def replace_linear_with_lora(model, rank, alpha):
    for name, module in model.named_children():
        if isinstance(module, torch.nn.Linear):
            # Replace the Linear layer with LinearWithLoRA
            setattr(model, name, LinearWithLoRA(module, rank, alpha))
        else:
            # Recursively apply the same function to child modules
            replace_linear_with_lora(module, rank, alpha)
